samples.ask: Has there been a time when you felt like Sahil? Link it to an event in the story.

samples.ask: What do you think of the captain who picked Sahil first the next day? Give your reasons.

samples.ask: How do you think Mariam felt on her first day in Pune? Link her feelings to a time when you were somewhere new.
samples.answer: I think Mariam felt lost and a bit scared, because everything was big and noisy. I felt the same on my first day at a new swimming class, where I did not know anybody and the pool looked huge.

samples.ask: The boy said he had never seen the sea. How did your feelings about him change by the end of the story? Explain why.

samples.answer: Dear Nani, Thank you for the new books. Their stories are very funny. We are going to Goa in May and I can't wait. There is a beach near our hotel. Love, Diya

samples.ask: Proofread this recount. Find and fix every mistake in spelling, grammar and punctuation.
samples.text: last week our class went to the zoo. We seen to tigers sleeping in the shade. The monkeys was jumping to and fro. I buyed a mango ice lolly becaus it was so hot
samples.answer: Last week our class went to the zoo. We saw two tigers sleeping in the shade. The monkeys were jumping to and fro. I bought a mango ice lolly because it was so hot.

samples.ask: Proofread this story opening. Find and fix every mistake in spelling, grammar and punctuation.
samples.text: One morning, sana woke up and look out of the windo. The hole street was full of water. where is the school bus? she asked. Her mother laughed and sayed their was no school today.
samples.answer: One morning, Sana woke up and looked out of the window. The whole street was full of water. "Where is the school bus?" she asked. Her mother laughed and said there was no school today.

samples.ask: Describe the school canteen at lunchtime in three or four sentences. Use what you see, hear and smell. Word bank: crowded, steaming, clatter, spicy.
samples.answer: The canteen is crowded at lunchtime. Steaming pots of dal sit on the long counter. I can hear the clatter of steel plates and the chatter of hungry children. The spicy smell of poha floats out of the door.
key_points: describes the canteen, not what happens next
uses sight, sound and smell
uses at least two words from the word bank

samples.ask: Describe Dada, the old balloon seller outside the school gate, in three or four sentences. Say how he looks and sounds. Word bank: wrinkled, cheerful, bright, squeaky.
samples.answer: Dada has a wrinkled face and a white moustache. He holds a bunch of bright balloons that bob above his head. His cheerful voice calls out to every child who passes. When he twists a balloon into a dog, it makes a squeaky noise.
key_points: describes how Dada looks
describes a sound
uses at least two words from the word bank

samples.ask: Describe your street on a rainy monsoon morning in three or four sentences. Use what you see, hear and feel. Word bank: puddles, drumming, grey, muddy.
samples.answer: The sky over our street is dark grey. Rain is drumming on the tin roofs of the shops. Big brown puddles fill the road, and the auto-rickshaws splash through them. My shoes feel cold and muddy.
key_points: describes the street, not a story
uses sight, sound and touch
uses at least two words from the word bank

samples.ask: Describe a railway station platform in Pune just before a train arrives. Write four or five sentences and use at least two senses.
samples.answer: The platform is packed with families and their heavy bags. A tea seller walks past shouting, "Chai, garam chai!" The smell of hot vada pav drifts from a small stall. Suddenly the rails begin to hum and a loud horn blows in the distance. Everyone picks up their bags and steps forward.
key_points: describes the platform with chosen details
uses at least two senses
keeps to the moment before the train arrives

samples.ask: Describe Tara, a new girl, on her first morning at a new school. Write four or five sentences so the reader can picture her and guess how she feels.
samples.answer: Tara stands by the classroom door in a uniform that is still stiff and new. She holds her school bag tightly with both hands. Her eyes dart from desk to desk, looking for a friendly face. When someone says hello, she gives a tiny smile and looks down at her shiny black shoes.
key_points: describes how Tara looks
shows her feelings through actions, not only by naming them
uses chosen words

samples.ask: Describe a busy vegetable market on a Sunday morning. Write four or five sentences and use at least two senses.
samples.answer: The vegetable market is noisy and crowded on Sunday morning. Sellers sit behind tall piles of red tomatoes, purple brinjals and green chillies. They shout their prices over the honking of scooters. The air smells of fresh coriander and wet earth. Shoppers squeeze past each other with heavy cloth bags.
key_points: describes the market with chosen details
uses at least two senses
does not turn into a list of events

samples.ask: Write the opening paragraph of a story that describes the old empty house at the end of Lane 4. Use three senses and one comparison, so the reader wants to find out more.
samples.answer: At the end of Lane 4 stands a house that nobody visits. Its windows are cracked like broken spectacles, and creepers have wrapped the gate in green ropes. When the wind blows, the door creaks open and slams shut again. The air near the steps smells of damp wood and old dust. Some evenings, a faint yellow light flickers in the attic, even though no one has lived there for years.
key_points: describes the house with chosen details
uses three senses
uses one comparison
ends with a detail that makes the reader want to read on

samples.ask: Describe Captain Raghav, the strict but fair captain of the school kabaddi team, so a reader can picture him. Include his looks, how he moves and speaks, and one comparison.
samples.answer: Captain Raghav is tall and broad, with short hair that stands up like a brush. He walks onto the field with long, firm steps, and the whole team goes quiet. His voice is deep and loud, but he never shouts at anyone who has tried their best. When a player is hurt, he kneels beside them and speaks gently. His eyes are sharp, so he notices every mistake and every good move.
key_points: describes his looks
describes how he moves and speaks
shows he is strict but fair
uses one comparison

samples.ask: Describe Diwali night as seen from the rooftop of a building. Use three senses and one comparison so the reader feels they are there.
samples.answer: From our rooftop, the whole city twinkles with lamps. Strings of lights hang from every balcony like glowing necklaces. Rockets whistle into the dark sky and burst into showers of gold and green. The smell of smoke mixes with the sweet smell of jalebis from the flat below. I can feel the warm air on my face as I hold my little sparkler tightly.
key_points: describes the scene with chosen details
uses three senses
uses one comparison
keeps to describing the moment

samples.ask: Describe a cave that no one has entered for a hundred years, and make it feel mysterious. Then write one sentence saying which detail you think will make the reader want to read on.
samples.answer: The mouth of the cave is hidden behind a curtain of thick roots. Inside, the air is cold and still, and every footstep echoes like a whisper coming back. Water drips from the roof and gathers in black pools that shine like glass. On the far wall, someone has carved strange shapes that look like eyes. Far away in the dark, something rattles softly and then stops. I think the carved eyes will make the reader want to read on, because they make us wonder who made them.
key_points: builds a mysterious mood with chosen details
uses more than one sense and a comparison
names one detail and explains why it hooks the reader

samples.ask: Describe a robot that works in a library, a character you have made up. Show its personality through how it looks and what it does.
samples.answer: Pustak is a short, round robot with a shiny copper body that is covered in tiny dents. Its two blue eyes glow softly, like lamps on a foggy night. It rolls silently between the shelves so that it never disturbs a reader. When a child cannot reach a book, Pustak stretches its long arm and hands it over with a little bow. If anyone speaks loudly, it raises one metal finger to the small speaker on its face and beeps, very politely, "Shhh."
key_points: describes an imagined character with chosen details
shows personality through actions
uses a comparison
every part of the task is there

samples.ask: Describe a night market as a small mouse would see it from the ground, so that everything seems huge.
samples.answer: From under the fruit stall, the night market is a forest of giant legs. Sandals as big as boats thump past my nose, and I have to dodge them quickly. Above me, lanterns hang like burning moons. The smell of roasted corn is so strong that my whiskers twitch. A peanut shell falls beside me with a crash like a falling rock. The roar of voices never stops, and I press myself against a cool, damp crate until the crowd moves on.
key_points: describes from the mouse's point of view throughout
makes ordinary things seem huge
uses several senses and comparisons
builds a clear mood

samples.ask: Write a new ending for the story. In your ending, the crow cannot find any pebbles. Begin with: The crow looked around, but there were no pebbles anywhere.
samples.answer: The crow looked around, but there were no pebbles anywhere. Then he saw a long, hollow straw lying near the tree. He picked it up in his beak and pushed it into the pot. He sucked hard, and the cool water came up the straw. The clever crow drank until he was full.
key_points: keeps the crow, the pot and the little water from the story
has no pebbles, and the crow solves the problem another way
finishes the story clearly

samples.ask: Write a new ending in which a girl from the village helps the crow. Begin with: Just then, a girl called Sita came to the tree.
samples.answer: Just then, a girl called Sita came to the tree with a jug of water. She saw the tired crow hopping around the pot. Gently, she poured fresh water into the pot until it was full. The crow drank happily. After that, he visited Sita every morning, and she always left water for him.
key_points: keeps the thirsty crow and the pot
Sita helps the crow
the ending finishes the story

samples.ask: Write a new beginning for the story that tells why the crow was so thirsty. Begin with: It was the hottest day of the summer.
samples.answer: It was the hottest day of the summer. The sun burned in the sky, and the ground cracked in the heat. The crow had flown all morning to find food for his babies. Now his throat was dry and sore, and he could not see a single drop of water anywhere.
key_points: explains why the crow is thirsty
leads into the story as it is
uses chosen words for the heat

samples.ask: Write a different ending for the story, starting from the moment the kite gets stuck. Do not use Mr Joshi in your ending.
samples.answer: Meera sat down on the terrace and felt like crying. Then Kabir had an idea. He tied a small stone to a piece of string and threw it gently over the branch. When it came down on the other side, he pulled slowly, and the branch bent low. Meera reached up and freed her kite. It was a little torn, so they mended it with tape and flew it together until sunset.
key_points: starts when the kite is stuck
does not use Mr Joshi
Meera and Kabir act as they do in the story
the problem is solved

samples.ask: Write a new beginning for the story that shows how Meera got her new red kite.
samples.answer: The day before Makar Sankranti, Meera went to the market with Aaji. Hundreds of kites hung from the stalls like coloured birds. Meera had saved her pocket money for weeks, but most kites cost too much. At the last stall, she found a bright red kite with a long tail. Aaji added the last ten rupees, and Meera took it home as carefully as an egg.
key_points: shows how Meera got the kite
leads into the story the next morning
uses chosen details

samples.ask: Write a different ending in which the kite string snaps and the kite floats away.
samples.answer: Meera tugged one more time, and suddenly the string snapped. The red kite floated free and drifted over the rooftops. Meera and Kabir watched it go, feeling sad. A few minutes later, a little girl on a nearby terrace caught it and waved happily. Meera smiled and waved back. Then Kabir gave her his own kite, and they flew it together until sunset.
key_points: the string snaps and the kite floats away
Meera and Kabir react as the story's characters would
the ending closes the story

samples.ask: Write a new ending for the story, starting from the moment Arjun finds the monkey. Make it fit Arjun, who is quiet but notices things.
samples.answer: Arjun did not shout or run at the monkey. Instead, he sat down quietly on a rock and watched it. He noticed that the monkey kept looking at a baby monkey hiding in a tree. Slowly, Arjun broke off a piece of thepla and placed it on the ground. The monkey took it to the baby and left the tiffin box behind. When Arjun told the class, his friends Zoya and Dev were amazed, and they shared their lunch with him.
key_points: starts when Arjun finds the monkey
Arjun stays quiet and notices a detail
fits what has already happened
the problem is solved clearly

samples.ask: Write a new beginning for the story that starts on the bus to the fort. Show the reader that Arjun is quiet but notices things.
samples.answer: The bus to Sinhagad Fort was full of noise. Everyone was singing and shouting, but Arjun sat by the window and said nothing. He was watching the hills. While the others played games, he spotted a hawk circling over the road and a family of monkeys sitting on a wall. He held his bag tightly on his lap, because his mother had packed his favourite theplas.
key_points: is set on the bus before the story begins
shows Arjun is quiet
shows Arjun notices things
leads into the rest of the story

samples.ask: Write a different ending in which the trail of crumbs leads Arjun to a surprise of your own. It must still fit what has already happened.
samples.answer: Arjun followed the crumbs quietly behind the wall. There, under a tree, sat a little stray dog with his tiffin box between its paws. The dog was very thin, and it wagged its tail weakly when it saw him. Arjun felt sorry for it, so he let it finish the theplas. When he told the class, Zoya and Dev shared their lunch with him, and the guide promised to take the dog to a shelter.
key_points: the crumbs lead to a new surprise
keeps Arjun quiet and kind
fits the trip and the missing tiffin
the ending closes the story

samples.ask: Write a different ending in which Gopal wishes for gold. Show what happens to him, so the ending still fits the story's message.
samples.answer: Gopal's eyes shone. "I wish for a room full of gold," he said. The old woman nodded and disappeared. The next morning, Gopal's hut was full of gold, but he was too busy counting it to make any pots. Soon the families had nothing to cook in, and the children stopped visiting. Gopal sat alone among his gold coins, feeling lonelier than ever. At last he picked up some clay, sat at his wheel and began to make a pot. As it turned, he smiled for the first time in weeks.
key_points: Gopal wishes for gold
shows what the wish costs him and the village
the ending still shows that helping people matters
fits Gopal and the old woman

samples.ask: Write a new ending told by the old woman, saying what she thought when Gopal made his wish.
samples.answer: I have granted many wishes, and most people ask for gold. When Gopal's eyes shone, I was sure he would ask for it too. Then I saw him look at his wheel and the pots drying in the sun. I watched him think of the children and the families. When he wished that his hands would always help people, my heart felt warm. I walked away into the dusk smiling, because I knew he had found what he was looking for.
key_points: told by the old woman in the first person
shows what she thought before and after the wish
keeps the same wish and events
fits the story's message

samples.ask: Write a new beginning that sets the story in a busy city today instead of a village long ago. Then write one sentence saying how this changes the story.
samples.answer: In a crowded street in Pune, between a phone shop and a tea stall, there was a tiny pottery shop. Gopal sat at his wheel every day while scooters roared past and buses honked. His pots were strong, but most people walked past to buy plastic buckets from the big stores. "If only I were rich like the shop owners on Main Road," he sighed. Setting the story in a city today makes Gopal's wish harder, because people there buy plastic instead of clay pots.
key_points: moves the setting to a city today
keeps Gopal a potter who wants to be rich
explains in one sentence how the change affects the story

samples.ask: Read about the peafowl. Fill in the table with short notes. Write only the key words.
Read about the peafowl. Fill in the table with short notes about its tail and its food.

answer.What they eat: seeds, insects, small snakes and berries

samples.ask: Read about the peafowl. Fill in the table with a few key words in each box.

answer.What a peacock does when it rains: spreads its tail like a fan and dances

samples.ask: Read about lassi. Make short notes in the table. Write only the words that answer each box.
Read about lassi. Make notes on what is added to each kind of lassi.
Read about lassi. Make short notes for a class poster about it.

answer.Why it is healthy: curd is good for the stomach

samples.ask: You are going to write a report about the monsoon. Make short notes for it in the table. Leave out details the report does not need.
You are making a poster called Why the Monsoon Matters. Make short notes for it in the table.
You are making a science poster on how monsoon rain is made. Make short notes in the table. Write key words, not sentences.

answer.When they drop it as rain: when they meet the land and hills

samples.ask: Make four short notes about the history of Sinhagad Fort. Then use your notes to write a short paragraph for a class display.
samples.answer: Notes: once called Kondhana; walls on cliff edges; 1670, Tanaji climbed cliffs at night; renamed Sinhagad, Lion's Fort. Paragraph: Sinhagad Fort was once called Kondhana. Its walls were built along the edges of the cliffs, so it was hard to attack. In 1670, the brave warrior Tanaji Malusare and his soldiers climbed the cliffs at night and captured it. Sadly, Tanaji died in the battle, so the fort was renamed Sinhagad, which means Lion's Fort.
key_points: four short notes on the history, not on visiting
notes are key words, not sentences
the paragraph uses every note in a sensible order

samples.ask: Make short notes on what visitors can see and do at the top of Sinhagad. Then use them to write a short guide for younger children.
samples.answer: Notes: old gates; water tanks cut in rock; Tanaji memorial; pithla bhakri and buttermilk at stalls. Guide: When you reach the top of Sinhagad, look for the old gates first. Next, find the water tanks that were cut into the rock long ago. Then visit the memorial to the brave warrior Tanaji. Before you walk back down, try some hot pithla bhakri and a glass of cool buttermilk from the stalls.
key_points: notes cover what to see and what to eat
notes are short
the guide uses the notes and suits younger children

samples.ask: Make short notes on when and how to visit Sinhagad. Then use them to write a short paragraph for the school newsletter about planning a family trip.
samples.answer: Notes: 30 km south-west of Pune; walk up path or go by road; best October to February; path slippery in monsoon. Paragraph: Sinhagad Fort is about thirty kilometres south-west of Pune, so it makes a good day trip. Families can walk up the winding path or travel most of the way by road. The best time to go is from October to February, when it is cool. Try not to go in the monsoon, because the path can be very slippery.
key_points: notes on where it is, how to get there and when to go
notes are short
the paragraph is written from the notes for families

samples.ask: Read the recount. Number these events in the order they happened. Use the linking words to help you.
options: they filled the petals with pink and yellow powder
they placed small clay lamps around the edge
Priya drew the outline of a lotus
answer: Priya drew the outline of a lotus
they filled the petals with pink and yellow powder
they placed small clay lamps around the edge

samples.ask: Read how Rohan grew a bean. Number these events in the order they happened.
options: a green shoot appeared at the top
he soaked a bean in water overnight
Rohan planted the bean in a pot of soil
a tiny white root pushed out of the bean
answer: he soaked a bean in water overnight
a tiny white root pushed out of the bean
a green shoot appeared at the top
Rohan planted the bean in a pot of soil

samples.ask: Read the recount of the zoo trip. Number these events in the order they happened.
options: we ate our tiffin under a big banyan tree
we saw the white tiger resting in the shade
everyone bought a postcard at the gate
we watched the elephants splashing in their pool
answer: we saw the white tiger resting in the shade
we ate our tiffin under a big banyan tree
we watched the elephants splashing in their pool
everyone bought a postcard at the gate

samples.ask: These sentences make a paragraph, but they are mixed up. Number them in the right order. Use the linking words to help you.
options: Luckily, his friend Farhan lent him a spare one.
Anil woke up late on the morning of the cricket match.
With Farhan's bat, Anil scored twenty runs and his team won.
Because he was in a hurry, he forgot to pack his bat.
When he reached the ground, he saw that it was missing.
answer: Anil woke up late on the morning of the cricket match.
Because he was in a hurry, he forgot to pack his bat.
When he reached the ground, he saw that it was missing.
Luckily, his friend Farhan lent him a spare one.
With Farhan's bat, Anil scored twenty runs and his team won.

samples.ask: These sentences tell why the class plants died, but they are mixed up. Number them in the right order.
options: While she was away, nobody remembered to water the plants.
In April, our class planted sunflower seeds in pots by the window.
As a result, when she came back, the leaves were brown and dry.
Every morning, Neha watered them, so they grew quickly.
Then Neha went to visit her grandmother in Nashik for two weeks.
answer: In April, our class planted sunflower seeds in pots by the window.
Every morning, Neha watered them, so they grew quickly.
Then Neha went to visit her grandmother in Nashik for two weeks.
While she was away, nobody remembered to water the plants.
As a result, when she came back, the leaves were brown and dry.

samples.ask: These steps for making poha are mixed up. Number them in the right order.
options: When the oil is hot, add mustard seeds, onion and curry leaves.
Finally, sprinkle coriander on top and serve it hot with lemon.
First, wash the flattened rice and leave it to soften.
Once the onion is soft, stir in the rice with salt and turmeric.
While it softens, heat a little oil in a pan.
answer: First, wash the flattened rice and leave it to soften.
While it softens, heat a little oil in a pan.
When the oil is hot, add mustard seeds, onion and curry leaves.
Once the onion is soft, stir in the rice with salt and turmeric.
Finally, sprinkle coriander on top and serve it hot with lemon.

samples.ask: Use these notes to write a paragraph about the school sports day. Put the ideas in order and link them with at least three different linking words.
samples.text: Notes: march around the field; younger classes' races; kabaddi final 4A v 4B, very close; prizes; everyone tidies up
samples.answer: Our school sports day began early in the morning with a march around the field. After the march, the younger classes ran their races while we cheered from the stands. Next came the event everyone was waiting for, the kabaddi final between Class 4A and Class 4B. It was so close that nobody knew who would win until the last raid. When the match was over, the principal gave out the prizes. Finally, everyone helped to tidy the field before going home.
key_points: uses every note in the right order
links ideas with at least three different linking words
each sentence follows on from the last

samples.ask: Use these notes to explain how to plant a tulsi sapling. Write a paragraph, not a list, and link each step to the one before.
samples.text: Notes: fill pot with soil; make hole; put sapling in, press soil; water; sunny spot (needs light)
samples.answer: Planting a tulsi sapling is easy if you follow the steps in order. First, fill a clay pot with soil, leaving a little space at the top. Then make a small hole in the middle with your finger. After that, place the sapling in the hole and press the soil gently around it so that it stands up straight. Once it is planted, water it well. Finally, put the pot in a sunny spot, because tulsi needs plenty of light to grow.
key_points: follows the steps in the order of the notes
uses at least three different linking words
is a paragraph, not a list

samples.ask: Use these notes to write a paragraph explaining why the school started a No Plastic Day. Show how each idea leads to the next.
samples.text: Notes: plastic thrown in canal; monsoon, drains blocked; road by gate floods; children miss school; class writes to principal; No Plastic Day every Friday
samples.answer: Last year, a lot of plastic bags and wrappers were thrown into the canal behind our school. When the monsoon came, the plastic blocked the drains. As a result, the water had nowhere to go, so the road near the school gate flooded. Many children could not get to school for two days. Because of this, our class wrote a letter to the principal. She agreed with us, and now every Friday is No Plastic Day.
key_points: explains the causes and results in order
uses linking words for cause and result, such as because and so
each idea leads to the next

samples.ask: Use these notes to write a paragraph explaining what happened to the village well. Use linking words for time, cause and contrast, such as because, as a result and however.
samples.text: Notes: well gave water for years; village grew, more pumps; well dried up; women walk to river; villagers build small walls to trap rain; well fills again
samples.answer: For many years, the well in Wadgaon gave sweet water to every family. However, when the village grew, people began to dig new wells and use pumps all day. Because so much water was taken out, the old well slowly became dry. As a result, the women had to walk two kilometres to the river every morning. The villagers decided to act. They built small walls across the stream to trap the monsoon rain, so the water soaked back into the ground. The next year, the old well filled up again.
key_points: explains causes and results in a logical order
uses links for time, cause and contrast
each idea builds on the one before
the ending shows the result of the villagers' action

samples.ask: These ideas are jumbled. Write them as one paragraph in a logical order. Then add one sentence explaining why you chose that order.
samples.text: Ideas: the poster wins first prize; Sana sees Ishan eating alone; Ishan helps make the poster because he is good at drawing; Sana invites him to sit with her friends; by Friday he smiles every morning
samples.answer: On Monday, Sana noticed that the new boy, Ishan, was eating lunch alone. She invited him to sit with her friends. Because Ishan was good at drawing, he helped them make a poster for the science fair. As a result, their poster won first prize, and Ishan became part of the group. However, the best part was that by Friday he was smiling every morning. I put the ideas in this order because each one happened because of the one before it.
key_points: puts the ideas in a logical order
links them with words for time, cause and contrast
explains why the order works

samples.ask: Write a paragraph explaining how a small seed can become a tall mango tree. Make clear how each stage leads to the next, and use at least one link for contrast.
samples.answer: A mango tree begins as a single seed inside the stone of a fruit. When the stone falls into damp soil, the seed soaks up water and begins to swell. Soon a root pushes down into the ground, so the seedling can drink. After that, a shoot grows upwards towards the light. Young mango plants grow slowly at first. However, once their roots are deep, they grow quickly. After about five years, the tree is tall enough to flower, and then the flowers turn into new mangoes.
key_points: explains each stage in order
shows how each stage leads to the next
uses at least one link for contrast
uses links for time and cause

samples.ask: Finish the scene. Write four more lines for Isha and Nikhil. Put one stage direction in brackets.
samples.text:
Scene: The school canteen.
ISHA: Nikhil, have you seen my tiffin box?
NIKHIL: (shaking his head) No. Where did you leave it?
samples.answer:
ISHA: (looking under the table) I put it right here before the bell.
NIKHIL: Look, there is a blue box on the window sill. Is that yours?
ISHA: Yes! I must have left it there when I opened the window.
NIKHIL: Quick, let us eat before the bell rings again.
key_points: four new lines, each with the speaker's name and a colon
at least one stage direction in brackets
the lines follow on from the first two

samples.ask: Finish the scene. Write four more lines for Grandpa and Aman. Put one stage direction in brackets.
samples.text:
Scene: A park on a rainy evening.
GRANDPA: (looking at the sky) Aman, those clouds are very dark.
AMAN: Is it going to rain?
GRANDPA: Any minute now. We should start walking home.
samples.answer:
AMAN: But Grandpa, we have no umbrella!
GRANDPA: (laughing) Then we will get wet together, like when I was a boy.
AMAN: Will Mum be cross?
GRANDPA: Not if we bring her hot bhajiyas on the way home.
key_points: four new lines with names and colons
at least one stage direction in brackets
the lines follow on from the start

samples.ask: Finish the scene. Write four more lines for Mrs Rao and Kiran. Put one stage direction in brackets.
samples.text:
Scene: A bus stop in the monsoon.
MRS RAO: Kiran, why are you standing in the rain?
KIRAN: (sadly) I missed the school bus, and I do not know how to get home.
samples.answer:
MRS RAO: Do not worry, Kiran. I can call your father from my phone.
KIRAN: (smiling) Thank you, Mrs Rao. His number is in my diary.
MRS RAO: Good. You can wait under my umbrella until he comes.
KIRAN: That is very kind of you.
key_points: four new lines with names and colons
at least one stage direction in brackets
the lines solve Kiran's problem

samples.ask: Write a short scene of six lines. Two friends, Sara and Yusuf, find a lost puppy outside the school gate. Use two stage directions in brackets.
samples.answer:
SARA: (pointing) Yusuf, look! There is a puppy under the bench.
YUSUF: It is shivering. It must be lost.
SARA: (kneeling down) Come here, little one. Do not be scared.
YUSUF: It has a red collar. Maybe there is a name on it.
SARA: It says Bruno, and there is a phone number too.
YUSUF: Let us take it to the guard so he can call the owner.
key_points: six lines for Sara and Yusuf, each with a name and a colon
two stage directions in brackets
a listener can follow what happens

samples.ask: Write a short scene of six lines between a fruit seller and a boy who has forgotten his money. Use two stage directions in brackets.
samples.answer:
SELLER: Six bananas. That will be thirty rupees, please.
BOY: (searching his pockets) Oh no! I have left my money at home.
SELLER: Where do you live?
BOY: Just in the next building, near the temple.
SELLER: (handing him the bag) Take the bananas. You can pay me tomorrow.
BOY: Thank you, Uncle! I will bring it first thing in the morning.
key_points: six lines with names and colons
two stage directions in brackets
the problem is clear and solved through talk

samples.ask: Write a short scene of six lines in which two sisters both want the last piece of barfi at Diwali. Use two stage directions in brackets.
samples.answer:
RIYA: (grabbing the plate) The last barfi is mine!
ANU: That is not fair. You have already had three.
RIYA: But I helped Mum make them.
ANU: (folding her arms) So did I. I stirred the milk for ages.
RIYA: All right. Let us cut it in half.
ANU: Good idea. Happy Diwali, Riya!
key_points: six lines with names and colons
two stage directions in brackets
a listener can follow the argument and how it ends

samples.ask: Write a short scene for three friends who are practising for the school play when one of them forgets her lines. Add a scene heading and at least two stage directions.
samples.answer:
Scene: The school hall, after lunch.
MEHA: (holding a script) Let us start again from the beginning.
ROHIT: I am the king, so I go first. Who dares to enter my palace?
ZOYA: (opening her mouth, then stopping) I am... I am...
MEHA: You are the brave farmer, Zoya. Remember?
ZOYA: (covering her face) I have forgotten everything!
ROHIT: Do not worry. Say it with me slowly.
ZOYA: I am the brave farmer, and I have come to ask for rain.
key_points: a scene heading
each line has a name and a colon, with no speech marks
at least two stage directions in brackets, in the present tense
a listener can follow the problem and how it is solved

samples.ask: Write a short scene in which a girl and her grandfather get lost in a crowded market during the Ganesh festival. Add a scene heading and at least two stage directions.
samples.answer:
Scene: A crowded street during the Ganesh festival.
ASHA: (holding his hand tightly) Ajoba, I cannot see our street any more.
AJOBA: Neither can I. There are so many people.
ASHA: The drums are so loud!
AJOBA: (looking around) We came past a sweet shop with a blue sign.
ASHA: (pointing) There it is, next to the big pandal!
AJOBA: Clever girl. Our lane is just behind it.
ASHA: Can we buy some modaks first?
key_points: a scene heading
names and colons on every line
at least two stage directions in brackets
the problem and its solution come out through talk

samples.ask: Write a short scene inside an auto-rickshaw. A driver, a mother and her son are hurrying to catch a train. Add a scene heading and at least two stage directions.
samples.answer:
Scene: An auto-rickshaw on a busy road in Pune.
MOTHER: (checking her watch) Our train leaves in fifteen minutes!
DRIVER: Do not worry, madam. I know a short cut.
SON: (bouncing in his seat) Faster, faster!
MOTHER: Sit still, Neel, or you will fall.
DRIVER: (turning into a lane) Here we are, the back gate of the station.
MOTHER: Thank you so much! Come on, Neel, run!
key_points: a scene heading
three characters, each line with a name and a colon
at least two stage directions in brackets
a listener can follow the hurry and the ending

samples.ask: Turn this story paragraph into a playscript scene. Use a scene heading, the characters' lines and stage directions instead of a narrator.
samples.text: Manish ran up the steps, shouting that he had won the drawing competition. His grandmother put down her book and asked what he had drawn. When he said it was the old banyan tree with her sitting under it, her eyes filled with tears, and she hugged him tightly.
samples.answer:
Scene: The front steps of a house. Evening.
MANISH: (rushing up the steps) Grandma, guess what? I won the drawing competition!
GRANDMA: (putting down her book) Oh, Manish! What did you draw?
MANISH: Our old banyan tree, with you sitting under it.
GRANDMA: (wiping her eyes) Me? Under our tree?
MANISH: Yes. The judge said it was full of love.
GRANDMA: (hugging him tightly) Then it is the best drawing in the world.
MANISH: (grinning) Can we hang it in the hall, next to the clock?
GRANDMA: Of course we can.
key_points: every event of the story is shown through lines or directions
no narration; directions in brackets in the present tense
names, colons and a scene heading
directions show feelings such as Grandma's tears

samples.ask: Write a scene on a spaceship where two astronauts disagree about which button to press. Use stage directions to show feelings the characters do not say aloud.
samples.answer:
Scene: The control room of a spaceship far from Earth.
KAVERI: (calmly) The red button will turn on the back-up engine.
ARYAN: (wiping sweat from his forehead) No, it is the green one. I read the manual.
KAVERI: (her hand shaking slightly) I am the captain. We press red.
ARYAN: (staring at the warning light) And if you are wrong?
KAVERI: (taking a deep breath) Then we try green. Ready?
ARYAN: (nodding slowly) Ready.
(Kaveri presses the red button. The lights flicker, then glow bright.)
ARYAN: (laughing with relief) You were right!
key_points: names, colons and a scene heading
directions show fear or relief that the lines do not say
the disagreement and its ending are clear through talk

samples.ask: Write a scene for three characters at a village well long ago, when a stranger arrives. Add a list of characters, a scene heading and stage directions.
samples.answer:
Characters: LALITA, a girl; GOVIND, her brother; STRANGER, an old traveller.
Scene: A village well at sunrise, long ago.
LALITA: (lowering the bucket) The rope is getting old, Govind.
GOVIND: Father will make a new one after the harvest.
(A tired STRANGER walks slowly towards the well, leaning on a stick.)
STRANGER: Children, may I have a little water? I have walked all night.
LALITA: (looking at Govind, then filling a cup) Of course. Please sit.
STRANGER: (drinking) You are kind. In return, let me fix your rope.
GOVIND: (surprised) You know how to make rope?
STRANGER: (smiling) I have made rope for kings.
key_points: a list of characters and a scene heading
names and colons on every line, no speech marks
stage directions show movement and feeling
the lines show each character's personality

samples.ask: Read the story. Fill in this story plan with short notes from the story.

answer.Ending: they played a game of carrom

samples.ask: Before writing a story, a writer plans who, where and when. Fill in this plan for the story with short notes.
Fill in this plan to show how the children's feelings change in the story. Use short notes from the story.

answer.How they felt at the end: the best Sunday of the monsoon

samples.ask: Plan a story about a lost puppy on a story mountain. Write a short note for each part: opening, build-up, problem, resolution and ending.
samples.answer:
Opening: Tanvi walks to school in rain.
Build-up: hears whimper under auto-rickshaw.
Problem: puppy hurt; she will be late.
Resolution: tells guard; dry it, call vet.
Ending: puppy becomes school pet, Bundi.
key_points: a note for all five parts
short notes, not full sentences
the parts follow in story order

samples.ask: Plan instructions for making a paper boat as a numbered list of steps. Write short notes, not full sentences.
samples.answer:
You need: one square sheet of paper.
1. Fold in half, top to bottom.
2. Fold corners to middle.
3. Fold bottom strips up.
4. Open into square, fold up.
5. Pull sides out; boat ready.
key_points: what you need, then numbered steps
short notes, not sentences
steps in the order they are done

samples.ask: Plan a report about your school library on a mind map. Write the topic in the middle and four branches with short notes.
samples.answer:
Middle: Our school library.
Branch 1, where: second floor, next to art room.
Branch 2, books: stories, science, poems, comics.
Branch 3, rules: quiet, two books a week.
Branch 4, best part: reading corner with cushions.
key_points: the topic in the middle
four branches, each a different part
short notes, not sentences

samples.ask: You are going to write a report about elephants. Choose the best way to plan it: a story mountain, a mind map, a table or a list of steps. Say which you chose and write your plan.
samples.answer:
I chose a table, because a report gives facts under headings.
Looks: grey, big ears, long trunk, tusks.
Food: grass, leaves, bark, fruit.
Home: forests in Kerala, Karnataka and Assam.
Family: herds led by oldest female.
key_points: chooses a frame that suits a report, such as a table or mind map
says which frame and why
short notes under clear headings

samples.ask: You are going to write a story set during the Holi festival in which something goes wrong. Choose the best way to plan it. Say which you chose and write your plan.
samples.answer:
I chose a story mountain, because a story has a problem and a solution.
Opening: Holi morning, Dev and friends with colours.
Build-up: water balloons ready on terrace.
Problem: balloon hits Grandma's white sari.
Resolution: Dev says sorry, washes it.
Ending: Grandma throws pink colour at Dev, all laugh.
key_points: chooses a story mountain or another story frame
says which and why
a note for every part, in order
short notes

samples.ask: You are going to write instructions telling a younger child how to wash their hands properly. Choose the best way to plan them. Say which you chose and write your plan.
samples.answer:
I chose a list of steps, because instructions must be done in order.
1. Wet hands.
2. Soap on hands.
3. Rub palms, backs, between fingers.
4. Count to twenty.
5. Rinse.
6. Dry on clean towel.
key_points: chooses a list of steps
says which and why
every step, in order
short notes a younger child could follow

samples.ask: Your class will write a letter to the principal asking for a school vegetable garden. Plan the letter in a way of your choice, and explain in one sentence why that plan suits a letter.
samples.answer:
Plan as a list of parts:
1. Greeting: Dear Mrs Kapoor.
2. Our view: we want a vegetable garden.
3. Reason 1: learn how food grows.
4. Reason 2: fresh vegetables for school lunch.
5. Offer: we will water it every day.
6. Ending: Yours sincerely, Class 4B.
A list of parts suits a letter because each part goes in a set order, from the greeting to the ending.
key_points: plans every part of a letter, including greeting, view, reasons and ending
short notes in order
explains why the plan suits a letter

samples.ask: Plan a story told as a diary over three days of a school camp. Explain how your plan keeps the days in order.
samples.answer:
Plan as a table with one row for each day.
Day 1, Friday: arrive at camp; tents by lake; scared of the dark.
Day 2, Saturday: rope climbing; get lost on nature walk; found by guide.
Day 3, Sunday: campfire songs; feel brave; sad to leave.
The table keeps the days in order, because each row is one day, and the feelings change from scared to brave.
key_points: a plan with a part for each day
short notes for events and feelings
explains how the plan keeps the order

samples.ask: Your friend planned a recipe for mango lassi on a story mountain. Explain why that plan does not suit a recipe, and plan it again in a better way.
samples.answer:
A story mountain does not suit a recipe, because a recipe has no problem or resolution; it needs a list of what you need and steps in order.
New plan:
You need: mango, curd, sugar, ice.
1. Peel and chop mango.
2. Put mango, curd and sugar in blender.
3. Blend until smooth.
4. Pour into glasses with ice.
key_points: explains why a story mountain does not suit a recipe
plans again with a list of ingredients and steps
short notes in the right order

samples.ask: Read the story. Fill in Nandini's character profile with words from the story.

answer.Looks: two long plaits tied with red ribbons

samples.ask: Read the story. Fill in these boxes of Nandini's profile with words from the story.

answer.Something she said: I miss my friends, but I think I will like it here

samples.ask: Read the story. Fill in the profile boxes with words from the story.
Read the story. Fill in Uncle Faiz's profile. For each box, find the detail in the story.

answer.Looks: a round man with a grey beard
answer.A detail that shows he is generous: slipped an extra toffee into their bags
answer.What he likes to say: A sweet day starts with a sweet

samples.ask: Read the story. Fill in Rukhsar's profile. For each box, find the detail in the story.

answer.A detail that shows she is clever: add up a whole bill in her head

samples.ask: Read the story. Fill in the boxes to show what each character likes doing when the shop is quiet.

answer.A detail that shows Rukhsar's dream: a paper aeroplane on the shelf above the till

samples.ask: Write a character profile of Aditya. Include his looks, personality, what he likes and a quote, and back each one with a detail from the story.
samples.answer:
Looks: Aditya is small and wiry, with a scar on his chin from an old fall.
Personality: He is a cheerful and caring captain. I know this because he never stops smiling, and he runs to help Pooja when she freezes.
Likes: He likes playing fair and as a team.
Quote: "We play fair, and we play together."
key_points: covers looks, personality, likes and a quote
each part is backed by a detail from the story
the quote is his own words

samples.ask: Write a character profile of Pooja for a story writer. Include her looks, personality, how she shows her feelings and a quote, each backed by the story.
samples.answer:
Looks: Pooja is the tallest girl in the class, with a long plait.
Personality: She is strong but nervous. The story shows this when she freezes at the start of the match.
Feelings: When she is worried, she chews the end of her plait.
Quote: Aditya says to her, "You are our best defender," so she is good at defending.
key_points: covers looks, personality and feelings
each part has a detail from the story
includes a quote from the story

samples.ask: Write a character profile of Sameer. Include his personality, what he likes, one thing he does for others, and a detail from the story for each.
samples.answer:
Personality: Sameer is funny and cheerful. He jokes all the time and even makes Coach Sharma laugh.
Likes: He likes making people happy, and he danced all the way back to the classroom after the team won.
Kind act: He always helps the younger children tie their laces before a game.
This shows that although he jokes, he is also kind.
key_points: covers personality, likes and a kind act
each part is backed by a detail from the story
notices that he is both funny and kind

samples.ask: Write a character profile of Ramu. The story does not say what he is like, so use clues from the story to work it out, and give the detail that shows each trait.
samples.answer:
Looks: Ramu is old and wears a khaki coat two sizes too big, with squeaky boots.
Personality: He is calm, because when Vikram laughs at him he only smiles. He is also wise and careful. He says, "Lights go out. A flame does not forget," and he is right, because the lights fail in the storm.
Likes: He likes doing things the old way, like taking his lantern every night.
Quote: "Lights go out. A flame does not forget."
key_points: works out traits the story does not state
gives a detail for each trait
covers looks, personality, likes and a quote

samples.ask: Write a character profile of Vikram that shows how he changes from the start of the story to the end. Back each point with a detail.
samples.answer:
Looks: Vikram is a young guard.
At the start: He is careless and a little rude. He laughs at Ramu's lantern and spends most nights playing games on his phone.
In the storm: He is scared, because his hands shake in the dark hallway.
At the end: He is honest and humble. He looks at the floor and says, "It was all Ramu Kaka." He has learned from Ramu, because he decides to take a lantern too.
key_points: shows Vikram at the start and at the end
explains the change
backs each point with a detail or quote

samples.ask: Write a profile of a new character, Ramu's granddaughter Lata, who will appear in the next story. Use details from this story to show how she is like her grandfather.
samples.answer:
Name: Lata, aged nine.
Looks: She has short hair and always wears her grandfather's old watch, which is too big for her wrist.
Personality: Like Ramu, she is calm and notices things others miss. She does not laugh at old ways, because she has heard the story of the lantern many times.
Likes: She likes torches, maps and solving puzzles.
Quote: "Grandpa says a flame does not forget, so I always take a torch."
In the next story, she could use her torch to help find something lost in the museum.
key_points: a new character with looks, personality, likes and a quote
links her clearly to Ramu using details from the story
says how the profile will help the next story

samples.ask: You are Bunty, a puppy who has just moved into a small flat in Pune. Write two or three sentences as Bunty, saying what you think of your new home and why. You can begin: I think this flat is …
samples.answer: I think this flat is the best home ever because there is a sunny balcony. I can watch the pigeons all day. But I do not like the lift, because it makes my tummy feel funny.
key_points: writes as Bunty, using I
gives an opinion of the flat
gives a reason with because

samples.ask: You are Aaji, a grandmother, seeing the school's new computer room for the first time. Write two or three sentences as Aaji, giving your opinion and a reason. You can begin: I think this room is …
samples.answer: I think this room is wonderful because the children can learn so many new things. When I was at school, we only had a slate and chalk. The screens are very bright, though, so I hope they rest their eyes.
key_points: writes as Aaji, using I
gives an opinion of the room
gives a reason

samples.ask: You are a mango seller at the market. Write two or three sentences as the seller, giving your opinion of the monsoon rain. You can begin: I think the rain is …
samples.answer: I think the rain is a nuisance for my stall because customers stay at home. My mangoes get wet and nobody stops to buy them. I wish it would rain only at night!
key_points: writes as the seller, using I
gives an opinion of the rain
gives a reason

samples.ask: Kabir thinks his neighbour, Mr Joshi, is always grumpy. Today Mr Joshi helped him rescue his kite. Write three or four sentences as Kabir, giving your opinion of Mr Joshi now, with a reason.
samples.answer: I used to think Mr Joshi was the grumpiest man in our building. He always frowned when we played cricket in the lane. But today he climbed onto the wall with his bamboo pole and saved my kite. Now I think he is kind, because he helped me even though I once broke his window.
key_points: writes as Kabir
gives a clear opinion of Mr Joshi
gives a reason with a detail

samples.ask: You are a monkey who lives at Sinhagad Fort. Write three or four sentences as the monkey, giving your opinion of the school children who visit, with a reason.
samples.answer: I think school children are the best visitors at the fort. They are noisy, but they always drop tasty crumbs from their tiffin boxes. Yesterday a boy left a whole thepla on a rock. I hope more classes come next week!
key_points: writes as the monkey
gives an opinion of the children
gives a reason with a detail

samples.ask: You are Tara, a new girl, at the end of your first day at a new school. Write three or four sentences as Tara, giving your opinion of the school, with a reason.
samples.answer: I was nervous this morning, but now I think my new school is friendly. At lunch, a girl called Nisha asked me to sit with her. She even shared her pickle with me. I think I will be happy here.
key_points: writes as Tara
gives a clear opinion of the school
gives a reason with a detail

samples.ask: You are the crow from The Thirsty Crow. Write a short paragraph as the crow giving your opinion of the village in the hot summer, with two reasons.
samples.answer: In my opinion, the village is a terrible place in summer. First, every pond has dried up, so a thirsty bird like me has nowhere to drink. I flew over the fields all afternoon and did not see a single drop. Also, the farmers keep their water pots inside their huts, so even the pots are hard to find. If I were in charge, I would leave a bowl of water under every tree.
key_points: writes as the crow throughout
gives one clear opinion of the village
gives two reasons, each with a detail

samples.ask: You are Pooja, a nervous kabaddi player. Write a short paragraph as Pooja giving your opinion of your captain, Aditya, with two reasons.
samples.answer: I think Aditya is the best captain our team could have. First, he always plays fair, and he reminds us before every match that we play together. Second, he believes in me even when I do not believe in myself. When I froze in the match, he ran to my side and told me I was the best defender. Because of him, I stopped the raider and we won.
key_points: writes as Pooja
gives one clear opinion of Aditya
gives two reasons, each with a detail

samples.ask: You are the old banyan tree in the school playground. Write a short paragraph as the tree giving your opinion of the children at break time, with two reasons.
samples.answer: I have stood in this playground for fifty years, and I think the children are the best part of my day. Firstly, they make me feel young again when they play hide-and-seek around my roots. Secondly, they look after me. Last week, a girl saw that someone had carved a name into my bark, and she told the educator straight away. However, I do wish they would stop swinging on my lowest branch!
key_points: writes as the tree throughout
gives a clear opinion of the children
gives two reasons with details

samples.ask: Meena loves the monsoon, but her brother Sahil hates it. Write a few sentences as Sahil, then a few as Meena, so that each opinion of the rainy street is clear.
samples.answer:
Sahil: I think the monsoon is the worst season of the year. The street turns into a muddy river, and every passing bus splashes my uniform. My shoes have been wet for a week, and I cannot even play cricket.
Meena: I think the monsoon is magical. The street smells of wet earth, and the trees are bright green again. I love jumping in the puddles on the way home, and Mum makes hot bhajiyas whenever it pours.
key_points: two opposite opinions of the same street
each written in the character's own voice
each opinion has at least two reasons or details

samples.ask: You are a visitor from a desert planet who has never seen rain. Write a short paragraph giving your opinion of a Pune street in the monsoon, with reasons.
samples.answer: On my planet, water is so rare that we keep it in tiny jars. So when I landed in Pune, I could not believe my eyes. Water falls from the sky here, for free! In my opinion, this is the richest city in the universe. The people, however, do not seem pleased. They hide under black umbrellas and grumble about wet shoes. I think they do not know how lucky they are, and I plan to fill my spaceship before I fly home.
key_points: writes as the visitor throughout
gives a clear opinion that fits a stranger to rain
gives reasons with details
notices another view and answers it

samples.ask: You are Vikram, the young guard who once laughed at old Ramu's lantern. Write a short paragraph as Vikram giving your opinion of Ramu now, and say what you thought before.
samples.answer: When I first joined the museum, I thought Ramu Kaka was a silly old man. Why take a lantern in a building full of lights? I even laughed at him. Now I think he is the wisest person I know. Firstly, he was ready for the storm when I was not. Secondly, he stayed calm and rang the alarm while my hands were shaking. From tonight, I take a lantern too, because I want to be like him.
key_points: writes as Vikram
shows both his old and new opinions
gives two reasons for the new opinion with details

samples.ask: Write a note to your class educator saying whether your class should have a reading corner. Use this frame: Dear …, I think … One reason is … Another reason is … From …
samples.answer:
Dear Mrs Pillai,
I think our class should have a reading corner. One reason is that we could read quietly when we finish our work early. Another reason is that we could share books from home with our friends.
From Rohan
key_points: states a view
gives two reasons
has a greeting and a sign-off

samples.ask: Write a note to your parents saying why you should be allowed to join the school kabaddi team. Use this frame: Dear …, I think … One reason is … Another reason is … From …
samples.answer:
Dear Mum and Dad,
I think I should join the school kabaddi team. One reason is that it will make me fit and strong. Another reason is that I will make new friends from other classes.
From Aarav
key_points: states a view
gives two reasons
has a greeting and a sign-off

samples.ask: Write a note to the school cook saying which dish should be served on Fridays. Use this frame: Dear …, I think … One reason is … Another reason is … From …
samples.answer:
Dear Mr Patil,
I think you should serve vegetable pulao on Fridays. One reason is that almost everyone in our class likes it. Another reason is that it has lots of vegetables, so it is healthy.
From Ishita
key_points: states a view
gives two reasons
has a greeting and a sign-off

samples.ask: Write a short note to the principal saying whether the school should have a longer lunch break. Give your view and two reasons.
samples.answer:
Dear Mrs Kapoor,
I think our school should have a longer lunch break. Firstly, many children have to rush their food and do not have time to finish their tiffin. Secondly, a longer break would give us time to play outside, so we would feel fresher in the afternoon lessons.
Thank you for reading my note.
From Diya, Class 4A
key_points: states one clear view
gives two reasons with details
writes politely to the principal with a greeting and ending

samples.ask: Write a short note to the principal asking for water coolers on every floor. Give your view and two reasons.
samples.answer:
Dear Mr Rao,
I think there should be a water cooler on every floor of the school. Firstly, in summer we get very thirsty, but the only cooler is on the ground floor. Secondly, children from the top floor are often late back to class because they have to walk all the way down.
Yours sincerely,
Kabir, Class 4C
key_points: states one clear view
gives two reasons with details
polite tone with greeting and ending

samples.ask: Write a short note to the librarian saying whether children should be allowed to take home two books a week instead of one. Give your view and two reasons.
samples.answer:
Dear Mrs Shah,
I think we should be allowed to take home two books a week. One reason is that many of us finish a book in two days and then have nothing to read. Another reason is that we could take one story book and one information book, so we would learn more.
Thank you,
Sneha, Class 4B
key_points: states one clear view
gives two reasons with details
suits the librarian as a reader

samples.ask: Write a short piece for the school newsletter, for parents, saying why children should walk or cycle to school. Give your view and two reasons with details.
samples.answer:
Dear Parents,
We believe that more children should walk or cycle to school. Firstly, it is good for our health. A fifteen-minute walk each morning helps us stay fit and wakes us up before lessons. Secondly, fewer cars at the gate would make the road safer and the air cleaner. Every morning, there is a long line of cars honking outside the school. Please think about walking with your child, even once a week.
From the Class 4 Green Team
key_points: states one clear view for parents
gives two reasons with details
polite tone and a fitting ending that asks parents to act

samples.ask: Write a notice for Class 1 children telling them why they should not waste water. Choose words that suit young children.
samples.answer:
Hello, Class 1!
Please do not waste water. Here is why. First, water is precious. In summer, some villages near Pune have very little, and children there walk a long way to fetch it. Second, it is easy to save water. Turn off the tap while you soap your hands, and only take the water you can drink. If we all help, there will be enough for everyone.
From your friends in Class 4
key_points: states the view clearly
gives two reasons with details
uses short sentences and words that suit young children

samples.ask: Write a short letter to the editor of a local newspaper saying the park near your school needs more dustbins. Give your view and two reasons.
samples.answer:
Dear Editor,
I am writing because the park on Lane 7, near our school, needs more dustbins. Firstly, there is only one bin, and it is always full, so people drop wrappers on the grass. Secondly, the rubbish is dangerous for the stray dogs and birds that eat it. Last week, I saw a crow tangled in a plastic bag. Please could the city put up at least three more bins?
Yours faithfully,
Anaya Desai, Class 4
key_points: states one clear view
gives two reasons with details
formal tone that suits a newspaper editor

samples.ask: Write to the principal saying the school should stop using plastic plates at the Diwali mela. Give two reasons, and answer one point someone might make against your view.
samples.answer:
Dear Mrs Kapoor,
I think our Diwali mela should stop using plastic plates. Firstly, last year the bins overflowed with plates, and many blew into the canal behind the school. Secondly, Diwali is a festival of light and joy, so we should not harm nature while we celebrate. Some people may say that leaf plates cost more. However, if every family brought one steel plate from home, it would cost nothing at all. Please think about trying this at the mela this year.
Yours sincerely,
Vihaan, Class 4A

samples.answer: Good morning, everyone. I believe that there should be no homework at weekends. The most important reason is that children need time to rest and be with their families. Weekends are when we visit grandparents, play outside and help at home. Also, we come back on Monday fresher and ready to learn. Some people say that without weekend homework, we will forget what we learned. However, we can read a book we enjoy, which keeps our minds busy without any worksheets. Thank you for listening.

samples.ask: Write the text for a leaflet telling tourists why they should visit Sinhagad Fort in the cool months. Give two reasons and say which matters most.
samples.answer:
Visit Sinhagad Fort this winter!
The best time to visit Sinhagad is from October to February. The most important reason is safety. In the monsoon, the steep path becomes slippery, but in the cool months it is dry and easy to climb. Another reason is the view. On clear winter days, you can see the Khadakwasla lake shining far below. When you reach the top, warm up with hot pithla bhakri from the stalls. Pack your walking shoes and come soon!
key_points: states a clear view for tourists
